atomic_modes.operational_signal: Mandated decision window has closed with no output; tie-break channel is explicit in published procedure; the channel was not used or was used past the window; the absence of decision has foreseeable downstream cost documented in pre-window analyses.

PNO.name: Informational Persistent Non-Optimality
PNO.definition: A persistent regime where decisions operate on distorted, filtered, or over-compressed representations of reality.

PNO.name: Incentive Persistent Non-Optimality
PNO.definition: A persistent regime where declared institutional objectives diverge from effective actor-level objectives.

PNO.name: Aggregation Persistent Non-Optimality
PNO.definition: A persistent regime where collective aggregation rules convert local preferences into unstable or non-optimal outcomes.

PNO.name: Coordination Persistent Non-Optimality
PNO.definition: A persistent regime where known improvements are not executed because coordination costs, vetoes, or responsibility diffusion dominate.

PNO.name: Temporal Persistent Non-Optimality
PNO.definition: A persistent regime where locally rational short-horizon decisions compound into long-horizon deterioration.

PNO.name: Inter-System Persistent Non-Optimality
PNO.definition: A persistent regime where multiple institutional systems or jurisdictions optimize locally and create global mismatch or spillover.

PNO.name: Anti-Consensus Persistent Non-Optimality
PNO.definition: A persistent regime where interaction among agents prevents convergence to a shared decision state or produces false/staged consensus.

game_theory_patterns.name: Prisoner's Dilemma
game_theory_patterns.definition: Mutual defection equilibrium despite a jointly better cooperative outcome.

game_theory_patterns.name: Stag Hunt
game_theory_patterns.definition: Coordination problem between risk-dominant and payoff-dominant equilibria.

game_theory_patterns.name: Chicken / Hawk-Dove
game_theory_patterns.definition: Escalation game where each party prefers the other to yield, creating brinkmanship risk.

game_theory_patterns.name: Principal-Agent Problem
game_theory_patterns.definition: Agent has discretion and incentives that diverge from the principal’s objective.

game_theory_patterns.name: Moral Hazard
game_theory_patterns.definition: Hidden action or risk transfer causes behavior that the risk-bearer would not choose.

game_theory_patterns.name: Adverse Selection
game_theory_patterns.definition: Hidden information causes low-quality or misaligned counterparties to be selected.

game_theory_patterns.name: War of Attrition
game_theory_patterns.definition: Agents incur delay costs while waiting for others to concede.

game_theory_patterns.name: Coordination Game Failure
game_theory_patterns.definition: Multiple equilibria exist, but agents fail to converge on the superior equilibrium.

game_theory_patterns.name: Repeated Game Cooperation Breakdown
game_theory_patterns.definition: Cooperation collapses over repeated interactions because trust, punishment, or monitoring fails.

game_theory_patterns.name: Signaling / Cheap Talk Failure
game_theory_patterns.definition: Signals fail to credibly transmit private information or intentions.

game_theory_patterns.name: Bayesian Game / Incomplete Information
game_theory_patterns.definition: Agents choose strategies under uncertainty about types, preferences, or payoffs of others.

game_theory_patterns.name: Coalition Formation Instability
game_theory_patterns.definition: Coalitions form, split, or block action due to unstable distribution of gains and veto power.

game_theory_patterns.name: Auction / Bidding Failure
game_theory_patterns.definition: Procurement or allocation mechanism induces strategic bidding, winner’s curse, collusion, or inefficient allocation.

game_theory_patterns.name: Matching Market Failure
game_theory_patterns.definition: Agents and positions/resources are mismatched because of preference revelation, constraints, or allocation rule defects.

game_theory_patterns.name: Evolutionary Strategy Lock-In
game_theory_patterns.definition: A strategy persists because it is locally stable, even when globally inferior alternatives exist.

social_media_layer.description: Social media platforms are modeled as environments that generate, amplify, distort and diffuse signals across Homo-MAS and government-management processes.

hm_extensions.name: Viral cascade distortion
hm_extensions.definition: Rapid amplification of a signal through platform dynamics distorts perceived importance, prevalence, or legitimacy.

hm_extensions.name: Narrative amplification loop
hm_extensions.definition: Repeated social reinforcement of a narrative increases its dominance independent of evidentiary quality.

hm_extensions.name: Algorithmic visibility bias
hm_extensions.definition: Platform ranking and recommendation systems make visible content appear socially or evidentially stronger than it is.

hm_extensions.name: Emotional contagion propagation
hm_extensions.definition: Affectively loaded content spreads emotional states across agents and alters decision-relevant perception.

hm_extensions.name: Polarization acceleration
hm_extensions.definition: Platform interaction dynamics increase distance between agent clusters faster than deliberative correction can reduce it.

hm_extensions.name: Attention hijacking dynamics
hm_extensions.definition: High-salience content captures system attention and reallocates agenda priority away from severity or evidence.

hm_extensions.name: Meme compression distortion
hm_extensions.definition: Complex policy or institutional realities are compressed into memetic units that remove decision-critical nuance.

hm_extensions.name: Synthetic consensus illusion
hm_extensions.definition: Coordinated or algorithmically amplified signals create the appearance of broad consensus without corresponding distributed agreement.

gt_extensions.name: Attention competition game
gt_extensions.definition: Agents compete for scarce collective attention, often optimizing salience over accuracy.

gt_extensions.name: Virality maximization game
gt_extensions.definition: Agents optimize content for spread, producing equilibria where transmissibility outranks truth or decision utility.

gt_extensions.name: Outrage equilibrium
gt_extensions.definition: A stable interaction regime where emotionally provocative content dominates because it yields higher engagement payoffs.

gt_extensions.name: Engagement versus truth tradeoff
gt_extensions.definition: Platform incentives reward engagement even when engagement conflicts with accurate belief formation.

gt_extensions.name: Narrative dominance game
gt_extensions.definition: Agents compete to make their framing the default interpretive structure for public and institutional reasoning.

legal_juridical_contour_layer.name: Legal / Juridical Contour Layer
legal_juridical_contour_layer.core_principle: Law is not treated as final truth. Law is modeled as a dynamic governance contour that can reduce errors, create errors, mask errors, delay decisions, or become an object of improvement.
key_theses: Legal correctness is not identical to governance optimality.
A decision may be legally compliant while the legal contour itself contributes to a management error.
Laws and procedures can lag behind the reality of necessary decisions.
Legal analysis must include feasible alternative legal or institutional designs.
Legal contours should be evaluated through Errorlogy taxonomy, not only through compliance.

formalization.interpretation: High LCJ_gap indicates that the existing legal contour is unable to support the required governance response without producing error modes.

legal_contour_error_types.name: Legal lag
legal_contour_error_types.definition: The legal norm or procedure lags behind the operational reality of the governance problem.

legal_contour_error_types.name: Procedural delay production
legal_contour_error_types.definition: Legal procedures systematically create delay that functions as de facto veto or avoidance.

legal_contour_error_types.name: Jurisdictional fragmentation
legal_contour_error_types.definition: Legal authority is split across institutions or territories in a way that mismatches the scope of the externality.

legal_contour_error_types.name: Procedural laundering
legal_contour_error_types.definition: Substantive critique is answered by formal compliance with legal or procedural checklists.

legal_contour_error_types.name: Legal insulation of accountability
legal_contour_error_types.definition: Delegation, formal competence boundaries or legal separation make accountability difficult to return to the originating actor.

legal_contour_error_types.name: Normative overconstraint
legal_contour_error_types.definition: Legal constraints are so rigid that they block adaptive governance even when a lower-error alternative exists.

legal_contour_error_types.name: Normative underconstraint
legal_contour_error_types.definition: Legal ambiguity or lack of procedural boundaries permits discretionary drift, capture or inconsistent execution.

legal_contour_error_types.name: Rights / efficiency false binary
legal_contour_error_types.definition: Legal discourse frames rights safeguards and operational effectiveness as mutually exclusive when design alternatives exist.

legal_contour_error_types.name: Precedent inertia
legal_contour_error_types.definition: Past legal or institutional practice controls a new problem despite changed facts or technologies.

legal_contour_error_types.name: Legal alternative omission
legal_contour_error_types.definition: The decision record treats current law as the only possible path and fails to evaluate feasible legal/institutional alternatives.

standard_questions: What is the current legal position?
What legal or procedural constraint shaped the decision?
Does the legal contour match the actual scope and speed of the governance problem?
Which Errorlogy modes are created or amplified by the legal contour?
What legal alternatives were feasible at the time?
What risks would each legal alternative create?
Does legal compliance hide substantive management error?

cognitive_competence_capacity_layer.name: Cognitive / Competence Capacity Layer
cognitive_competence_capacity_layer.core_principle: Government-management errors emerge when the complexity of a task exceeds the collective cognitive, professional, informational and institutional capacity of the governance system that must process it.
cognitive_competence_capacity_layer.central_thesis: Complexity distribution, competence distribution and power/veto distribution are not the same. Errors arise when high-complexity tasks are routed through agents, procedures or legal contours whose capacity is below the level required for accurate understanding, rapid information exchange, coordination and correction.

cognitive_capacity_inequality.principle: Cognitive and competence capacities are unevenly distributed among homo-agents. General cognitive ability, domain expertise, systems thinking, uncertainty processing and metacognitive calibration differ across agents. In public-facing analysis, this should be framed as capacity mismatch rather than personal insult.

distribution_heuristics.name: Gaussian middle-mass heuristic
distribution_heuristics.description: Many agents in large bureaucratic systems are expected to cluster around ordinary or mid-level competence for a given task domain; this does not imply moral inferiority, only capacity distribution.

distribution_heuristics.name: Right-tail scarcity heuristic
distribution_heuristics.description: Agents capable of handling highly abstract, multi-domain, non-linear, fast-changing tasks are scarce; they form a right-tail capacity group relative to the task.

distribution_heuristics.name: Power-capacity mismatch heuristic
distribution_heuristics.description: Formal decision rights, status, seniority, legal authority or veto power often do not align with the right-tail competence needed for high-complexity tasks.

distribution_heuristics.name: Cognitive capitalism pressure heuristic
distribution_heuristics.description: In the era of cognitive capitalism, value and power increasingly depend on speed of cognition, information processing, model-building, AI literacy, systems thinking and ability to act under uncertainty. This makes cognitive-capacity inequality governance-relevant.

cognitive_capacity_inequality.public_language_rule: Avoid direct labeling such as 'low IQ official' unless a legitimate measured context exists. Prefer: 'capacity mismatch', 'insufficient task-relevant competence', 'limited cognitive bandwidth for the task', 'misrouting of complexity', or 'veto power not matched by task competence'.
cognitive_capacity_inequality.internal_modeling_note: IQ or general cognitive ability can be modeled as one latent variable of cognitive capacity, but it must not be treated as the only determinant of competence. Domain expertise, metacognition, calibration, institutional learning and information access are distinct variables.

formalization.Collective_Capacity: CGI = f(agent_capacity, information_velocity, transparency, coordination_quality, expert_routing, institutional_learning, legal_adaptivity, blocker_control)
formalization.Correction_Capacity: CC = Transparency * Information_Velocity * Competence_Routing * Expert_Access * Blocker_Removal * Feedback_Speed * Legal_Adaptivity

key_variables.name: domain_competence

key_variables.name: systems_thinking

key_variables.name: uncertainty_processing

key_variables.name: forecast_calibration

key_variables.description: Probability that an agent will block improvement due to misunderstanding, personal interest, status defense, legal formalism or factional incentives.

key_variables.name: legal_adaptivity
key_variables.description: Ability of the legal contour to adapt to task complexity without producing legal lag or procedural paralysis.

key_variables.name: AI_literacy
key_variables.description: Ability of governance agents to understand, procure, regulate and audit AI systems without overtrust, panic or procedural fiction.

capacity_mismatch_error_types.name: Task complexity exceeds governance capacity
capacity_mismatch_error_types.definition: The task requires more cognitive, technical, legal, institutional or coordination capacity than the governance system can provide.

capacity_mismatch_error_types.name: Power-capacity mismatch
capacity_mismatch_error_types.definition: Agents with high formal authority or veto power lack task-relevant capacity, while more competent agents lack decision power.

capacity_mismatch_error_types.name: Right-tail expertise exclusion
capacity_mismatch_error_types.definition: Rare high-capacity experts are excluded, underweighted, delayed or subordinated to average-capacity procedural actors.

capacity_mismatch_error_types.name: Blocker-agent induced error persistence
capacity_mismatch_error_types.definition: Agents with veto/delay power prevent error correction due to misunderstanding, incentives, status defense or legal-procedural control.

capacity_mismatch_error_types.name: Information velocity deficit
capacity_mismatch_error_types.definition: Relevant information moves too slowly or through too many lossy layers to correct the error before it compounds.

capacity_mismatch_error_types.name: Transparency deficit
capacity_mismatch_error_types.definition: The system cannot see its own error chain because evidence, dissent, responsibility or decision logic is opaque.

capacity_mismatch_error_types.name: Competence-routing failure
capacity_mismatch_error_types.definition: Complex tasks are routed by hierarchy, formal competence or political convenience instead of task-relevant expertise.

capacity_mismatch_error_types.name: Overconfidence under complexity
capacity_mismatch_error_types.definition: Agents underestimate the complexity of the task and overestimate their own understanding or model validity.

capacity_mismatch_error_types.name: Cognitive-capitalism lag
capacity_mismatch_error_types.definition: The governance system operates at a lower cognitive and information-processing speed than the AI/data/social-media environment it must govern.

capacity_mismatch_error_types.name: Correction-capacity collapse
capacity_mismatch_error_types.definition: The system lacks the combined transparency, speed, expert routing, legal adaptivity and blocker removal needed to correct known errors.

betterment_links.name: Increase transparency
betterment_links.effect: Reduces representation loss and procedural laundering.

betterment_links.name: Increase information velocity
betterment_links.effect: Reduces temporal compounding by shortening feedback loops.

betterment_links.name: Competence routing / expert escalation
betterment_links.effect: Routes high-complexity tasks to agents with adequate task-specific capacity.

betterment_links.name: Blocker removal / veto limitation
betterment_links.effect: Reduces delay-as-veto and deadlock produced by low-capacity or misaligned blocker-agents.

betterment_links.name: Legal adaptivity
betterment_links.effect: Reduces legal lag and normative overconstraint in fast-changing environments.

betterment_links.name: AI-assisted governance augmentation
betterment_links.effect: Increases collective processing capacity, but requires safeguards against automation bias and Goodhart effects.

anti_overclaim_rules: Do not reduce competence to IQ alone.
Do not use cognitive-capacity analysis as personal insult or deterministic ranking.
Separate measured competence, inferred competence and task-specific capacity.
Capacity mismatch is an analytic governance concept, not a legal guilt finding.
Right-tail expertise scarcity does not imply that experts should be unchecked; it implies better routing, review and accountability.
cognitive_competence_capacity_layer.public_explanation_template: The error likely emerged because the task was more complex than the governance contour processing it. Relevant information moved too slowly or opaquely, expertise was not routed to where power existed, and agents with veto or delay power could block correction. This is described as capacity mismatch, not as personal blame.

mechanism_pathologies_extended.name: Majority tyranny
mechanism_pathologies_extended.definition: Majority aggregation systematically overrides minority rights, constraints or legitimate interests.

mechanism_pathologies_extended.name: Minority capture
mechanism_pathologies_extended.definition: A small group captures decision rules, veto points or agenda access disproportionate to its public mandate.

mechanism_pathologies_extended.name: Strategic abstention equilibrium
mechanism_pathologies_extended.definition: Actors abstain to alter quorum, legitimacy, or responsibility distribution.

mechanism_pathologies_extended.name: Turnout distortion equilibrium
mechanism_pathologies_extended.definition: Outcome depends more on participation asymmetry than stable underlying preferences.

mechanism_pathologies_extended.name: Coalition cycling
mechanism_pathologies_extended.definition: Coalitions repeatedly reconfigure, preventing stable implementation or coherent policy trajectory.

mechanism_pathologies_extended.name: Preference misrepresentation equilibrium
mechanism_pathologies_extended.definition: Actors strategically misstate preferences because truthful revelation is punished or exploited.

mechanism_pathologies_extended.name: Voting paradox under uncertainty
mechanism_pathologies_extended.definition: Uncertainty over states or preferences makes collective voting produce unstable or misleading outcomes.

mechanism_pathologies_extended.name: Agenda truncation failure
mechanism_pathologies_extended.definition: Relevant options are removed from the agenda, causing the chosen alternative to be locally valid but globally inferior.

mechanism_pathologies_extended.name: Sequential voting distortion
mechanism_pathologies_extended.definition: The order of votes, amendments or procedural steps changes the substantive outcome.

mechanism_pathologies_extended.name: Coordination collapse under noise
mechanism_pathologies_extended.definition: Agents lose synchronization because noise overwhelms shared situational awareness.

mechanism_pathologies_extended.name: Threshold failure dynamics
mechanism_pathologies_extended.definition: A policy fails because activation thresholds, participation thresholds or capacity thresholds are not reached.

mechanism_pathologies_extended.name: Critical mass instability
mechanism_pathologies_extended.definition: A system oscillates around the critical mass needed for self-sustaining implementation.

mechanism_pathologies_extended.name: Coordination fatigue equilibrium
mechanism_pathologies_extended.definition: Repeated coordination attempts exhaust agents and normalize partial failure.

mechanism_pathologies_extended.name: Trust erosion feedback loop
mechanism_pathologies_extended.definition: Low trust causes defensive behavior that further reduces trust and coordination.

mechanism_pathologies_extended.name: Signal dilution
mechanism_pathologies_extended.definition: Decision-relevant signals are diluted through aggregation, reporting or excessive averaging.

mechanism_pathologies_extended.name: Information bottleneck collapse
mechanism_pathologies_extended.definition: A narrow reporting or approval channel cannot process the volume/complexity of decision-relevant information.

mechanism_pathologies_extended.name: Bayesian aggregation failure
mechanism_pathologies_extended.definition: Collective updating fails to approximate rational belief updating under dispersed evidence.

mechanism_pathologies_extended.name: Overweighting of early signals
mechanism_pathologies_extended.definition: Early signals disproportionately determine later collective belief and institutional action.

mechanism_pathologies_extended.name: Expert overdominance distortion
mechanism_pathologies_extended.definition: A single expert group or epistemic faction dominates beyond the reliability of its evidence.

mechanism_pathologies_extended.name: Institutional inertia lock-in
mechanism_pathologies_extended.definition: Existing institutional routines persist despite evidence that they no longer fit the task.

mechanism_pathologies_extended.name: Path dependence trap
mechanism_pathologies_extended.definition: Early choices constrain later options and lock the system into a suboptimal trajectory.

mechanism_pathologies_extended.name: Reform paradox
mechanism_pathologies_extended.definition: Attempted reform increases instability or coordination costs enough to block or reverse improvement.

mechanism_pathologies_extended.name: Overconstraint failure
mechanism_pathologies_extended.definition: Rules constrain action so tightly that the system cannot adapt to the task.

mechanism_pathologies_extended.name: Underconstraint chaos
mechanism_pathologies_extended.definition: Insufficient constraints allow inconsistent, arbitrary or capture-prone execution.

mechanism_pathologies_extended.name: Cross-system misalignment
mechanism_pathologies_extended.definition: Different systems optimize incompatible objectives while interacting over the same problem.

mechanism_pathologies_extended.name: Regulatory fragmentation
mechanism_pathologies_extended.definition: Regulatory regimes fragment the problem into pieces that cannot be governed coherently.

mechanism_pathologies_extended.name: Jurisdictional competition trap
mechanism_pathologies_extended.definition: Jurisdictions compete in ways that collectively degrade the governance outcome.

mechanism_pathologies_extended.name: Inter-system Nash conflict
mechanism_pathologies_extended.definition: Multiple systems settle into a Nash equilibrium that is globally inferior but locally stable.

mechanism_pathologies_extended.name: Policy spillover instability
mechanism_pathologies_extended.definition: A policy stabilizes one subsystem while destabilizing another through externalities.

mechanism_pathologies_extended.name: Delayed feedback instability
mechanism_pathologies_extended.definition: Feedback arrives after the system has already compounded the initial error.

mechanism_pathologies_extended.name: Oscillatory governance cycles
mechanism_pathologies_extended.definition: Policy alternates between overcorrection and reversal instead of converging.

homo_mas_interaction_pathologies.name: Influence asymmetry distortion
homo_mas_interaction_pathologies.definition: Influence in the Homo-MAS is disproportionate to competence, evidence or public mandate.

homo_mas_interaction_pathologies.name: Narrative dominance cascade
homo_mas_interaction_pathologies.definition: One narrative becomes dominant through agent interactions before evidence is adequately evaluated.

homo_mas_interaction_pathologies.name: Belief fragmentation
homo_mas_interaction_pathologies.definition: Agent clusters develop incompatible models of reality and cannot update toward a shared frame.

homo_mas_interaction_pathologies.name: Cognitive desynchronization
homo_mas_interaction_pathologies.definition: Agents operate with different time horizons, assumptions and problem representations.

homo_mas_interaction_pathologies.name: Strategic miscommunication equilibrium
homo_mas_interaction_pathologies.definition: Agents communicate ambiguously or selectively because truthful communication is strategically costly.

homo_mas_interaction_pathologies.name: Feedback loop amplification
homo_mas_interaction_pathologies.definition: Agent interactions amplify small errors into system-level distortions.

homo_mas_interaction_pathologies.name: Echo chamber reinforcement
homo_mas_interaction_pathologies.definition: Agents repeatedly validate each other inside a closed belief cluster.

homo_mas_interaction_pathologies.name: Cross-agent misalignment persistence
homo_mas_interaction_pathologies.definition: Persistent misalignment survives repeated interaction because incentives or identities prevent convergence.

homo_mas_interaction_pathologies.name: Trust network collapse
homo_mas_interaction_pathologies.definition: Breakdown of trust networks prevents credible information transfer and coordinated action.

homo_mas_interaction_pathologies.name: Coordination illusion failure
homo_mas_interaction_pathologies.definition: Agents believe coordination exists, but operational dependencies remain unresolved.

homo_mas_interaction_pathologies.name: Distributed ignorance equilibrium
homo_mas_interaction_pathologies.definition: No single agent sees the full system; each assumes another part of the system has the missing knowledge.

homo_mas_interaction_pathologies.name: System-wide belief bifurcation
homo_mas_interaction_pathologies.definition: The Homo-MAS splits into two or more incompatible belief regimes.

homo_mas_interaction_pathologies.name: Viral cascade distortion
homo_mas_interaction_pathologies.definition: Rapid amplification of a signal through platform dynamics distorts perceived importance, prevalence, or legitimacy.

homo_mas_interaction_pathologies.name: Narrative amplification loop
homo_mas_interaction_pathologies.definition: Repeated social reinforcement of a narrative increases its dominance independent of evidentiary quality.

homo_mas_interaction_pathologies.name: Algorithmic visibility bias
homo_mas_interaction_pathologies.definition: Platform ranking and recommendation systems make visible content appear socially or evidentially stronger than it is.

homo_mas_interaction_pathologies.name: Emotional contagion propagation
homo_mas_interaction_pathologies.definition: Affectively loaded content spreads emotional states across agents and alters decision-relevant perception.

homo_mas_interaction_pathologies.name: Polarization acceleration
homo_mas_interaction_pathologies.definition: Platform interaction dynamics increase distance between agent clusters faster than deliberative correction can reduce it.

homo_mas_interaction_pathologies.name: Attention hijacking dynamics
homo_mas_interaction_pathologies.definition: High-salience content captures system attention and reallocates agenda priority away from severity or evidence.

homo_mas_interaction_pathologies.name: Meme compression distortion
homo_mas_interaction_pathologies.definition: Complex policy or institutional realities are compressed into memetic units that remove decision-critical nuance.

homo_mas_interaction_pathologies.name: Synthetic consensus illusion
homo_mas_interaction_pathologies.definition: Coordinated or algorithmically amplified signals create the appearance of broad consensus without corresponding distributed agreement.

game_theory_patterns_extended.name: Signaling equilibrium breakdown
game_theory_patterns_extended.definition: Signals fail to distinguish true types/states, causing distorted collective inference.

game_theory_patterns_extended.name: Screening failure
game_theory_patterns_extended.definition: The mechanism fails to elicit or separate relevant types, qualifications or risks.

game_theory_patterns_extended.name: Information asymmetry cascade
game_theory_patterns_extended.definition: Hidden information triggers a sequence of defensive or adverse selections.

game_theory_patterns_extended.name: Bayesian misbelief equilibrium
game_theory_patterns_extended.definition: Agents settle into mutually reinforcing wrong beliefs under incomplete information.

game_theory_patterns_extended.name: Principal-agent multi-layer distortion
game_theory_patterns_extended.definition: Delegated agents optimize layer-specific goals across several chains of delegation.

game_theory_patterns_extended.name: Moral hazard escalation
game_theory_patterns_extended.definition: Protected actors take greater risks because costs are shifted elsewhere.

game_theory_patterns_extended.name: Adverse selection spiral
game_theory_patterns_extended.definition: Bad types or low-quality options increasingly dominate because quality is hard to observe.

game_theory_patterns_extended.name: Rent-seeking equilibrium
game_theory_patterns_extended.definition: Agents invest in capturing rents rather than increasing public value.

game_theory_patterns_extended.name: Regulatory capture equilibrium
game_theory_patterns_extended.definition: Regulated or interested actors systematically shape the regulator's behavior.

game_theory_patterns_extended.name: Repeated defection equilibrium
game_theory_patterns_extended.definition: Repeated interaction fails to sustain cooperation and normalizes defection.

game_theory_patterns_extended.name: Collapse of cooperation equilibrium
game_theory_patterns_extended.definition: Trust or enforcement failure shifts the system from cooperation to stable non-cooperation.

game_theory_patterns_extended.name: Reputation failure dynamics
game_theory_patterns_extended.definition: Reputation no longer rewards reliability or punishes opportunism adequately.

game_theory_patterns_extended.name: Grim trigger instability
game_theory_patterns_extended.definition: A single defection or perceived defection triggers persistent punishment and coordination loss.

game_theory_patterns_extended.name: Electoral competition distortion
game_theory_patterns_extended.definition: Electoral incentives distort policy selection away from long-term public value.

game_theory_patterns_extended.name: Populism equilibrium
game_theory_patterns_extended.definition: Actors converge on high-salience simplified policies because they dominate attention/payoff space.

game_theory_patterns_extended.name: Policy cycling game
game_theory_patterns_extended.definition: Policy repeatedly reverses as coalitions and incentives shift.

game_theory_patterns_extended.name: Coalition bargaining deadlock
game_theory_patterns_extended.definition: Coalitional bargaining generates a stable blocking equilibrium.

game_theory_patterns_extended.name: Strategic polarization equilibrium
game_theory_patterns_extended.definition: Actors benefit from increasing polarization, preventing convergence.

game_theory_patterns_extended.name: Multi-agent coordination failure
game_theory_patterns_extended.definition: Several agents fail to coordinate even when all prefer coordination to failure.

game_theory_patterns_extended.name: Anti-coordination equilibrium
game_theory_patterns_extended.definition: Agents benefit from differentiating or opposing, causing structured divergence.

game_theory_patterns_extended.name: Network game contagion
game_theory_patterns_extended.definition: Strategies and beliefs spread through a network and amplify local distortions.

game_theory_patterns_extended.name: Influence maximization distortion
game_theory_patterns_extended.definition: Agents optimize influence reach rather than truth, competence or public value.

game_theory_patterns_extended.name: Strategic misinformation equilibrium
game_theory_patterns_extended.definition: Misinformation persists because it offers strategic payoff to actors.

game_theory_patterns_extended.name: Attention economy equilibrium
game_theory_patterns_extended.definition: Attention-maximizing strategies dominate decision-relevant information.

game_theory_patterns_extended.name: Institutional game lock-in
game_theory_patterns_extended.definition: Institutions are trapped in stable strategic patterns that resist improvement.

main_equations.betterment: B* = argmin E_total(alternative) under feasible constraints

public_principles: Legal compliance is not identical to governance optimality.
Truth is fuzzy and incomplete; use μ, confidence, evidence grade and counterfactuals.
Analyze contribution of strategies, not moral blame by default.
Always include how it could have been done better.
Capacity mismatch is a governance concept, not a personal insult.
Platforms are environments and amplifiers, not errors by themselves.

max_mode_universe.name: Confirmation bias
max_mode_universe.definition: Tendency to search for, interpret, and recall information that confirms one's prior beliefs.

max_mode_universe.name: Anchoring
max_mode_universe.definition: Over-reliance on the first piece of numerical information encountered when making subsequent estimates.

max_mode_universe.name: Availability heuristic
max_mode_universe.definition: Judging the probability of an event by how easily examples come to mind.

max_mode_universe.name: Representativeness heuristic
max_mode_universe.definition: Judging probability by how much an outcome resembles a mental prototype, neglecting base rates.

max_mode_universe.name: Base-rate neglect
max_mode_universe.definition: Ignoring general statistical information in favor of case-specific information.

max_mode_universe.name: Dunning–Kruger effect
max_mode_universe.definition: People with low ability in a domain overestimate their competence in that domain.

max_mode_universe.name: Overconfidence effect
max_mode_universe.definition: Subjective confidence in one's judgments is reliably greater than objective accuracy.

max_mode_universe.name: Planning fallacy
max_mode_universe.definition: Systematic underestimation of the time, cost, and risk of future actions.

max_mode_universe.name: Optimism bias
max_mode_universe.definition: Tendency to believe one is less likely than others to experience a negative event.

max_mode_universe.name: Sunk-cost fallacy
max_mode_universe.definition: Continuing an endeavor because of previously invested resources, rather than marginal future value.

max_mode_universe.name: Status quo bias
max_mode_universe.definition: Preference for the current state of affairs, treating change as a loss.

max_mode_universe.name: Endowment effect
max_mode_universe.definition: People demand more to give up something than they would pay to acquire it.

max_mode_universe.name: Loss aversion
max_mode_universe.definition: Losses are psychologically about twice as powerful as equivalent gains.

max_mode_universe.name: Framing effect
max_mode_universe.definition: Different presentations of the same information produce different decisions.

max_mode_universe.name: Hindsight bias
max_mode_universe.definition: Tendency to see past events as having been predictable.

max_mode_universe.name: Outcome bias
max_mode_universe.definition: Judging a decision by its outcome rather than by the quality of the decision at the time.

max_mode_universe.name: Survivorship bias
max_mode_universe.definition: Focusing on entities that passed a selection process and overlooking those that did not.

max_mode_universe.name: Selection bias (in evaluation)
max_mode_universe.definition: Conclusions drawn from a non-representative sample.

max_mode_universe.name: Groupthink
max_mode_universe.definition: Pressure for unanimity in a cohesive group overrides realistic appraisal of alternatives.

max_mode_universe.name: Authority bias
max_mode_universe.definition: Tendency to attribute greater accuracy to the opinion of an authority figure.

max_mode_universe.name: In-group bias
max_mode_universe.definition: Favoring members of one's own group.

max_mode_universe.name: Out-group homogeneity effect
max_mode_universe.definition: Perceiving out-group members as more similar to each other than in-group members are.

max_mode_universe.name: Halo effect
max_mode_universe.definition: Overall impression of a person or entity influences judgment of specific traits.

max_mode_universe.name: Horn effect
max_mode_universe.definition: Negative trait generalizes to unrelated traits.

max_mode_universe.name: Bandwagon effect
max_mode_universe.definition: Adoption of a belief because many others hold it.

max_mode_universe.name: False consensus effect
max_mode_universe.definition: Overestimating the extent to which others share one's views.

max_mode_universe.name: Pluralistic ignorance
max_mode_universe.definition: Privately held disagreement with a norm while publicly going along, in the mistaken belief one is alone.

max_mode_universe.name: Conformity bias
max_mode_universe.definition: Alignment of expressed views with group consensus under social pressure.

max_mode_universe.name: Just-world hypothesis
max_mode_universe.definition: Belief that people get what they deserve.

max_mode_universe.name: Fundamental attribution error
max_mode_universe.definition: Over-attributing others' behavior to disposition, under-attributing to situation.

max_mode_universe.name: Actor–observer bias
max_mode_universe.definition: Attributing own behavior to context and others' to disposition.

max_mode_universe.name: Self-serving bias
max_mode_universe.definition: Crediting successes to self, blaming failures on circumstances.

max_mode_universe.name: Ultimate attribution error
max_mode_universe.definition: Group-level extension of attribution biases, favorable to in-group.

max_mode_universe.name: Illusion of control
max_mode_universe.definition: Overestimation of one's ability to control outcomes.

max_mode_universe.name: Illusion of explanatory depth
max_mode_universe.definition: People feel they understand complex systems more deeply than they do.

max_mode_universe.name: Illusion of validity
max_mode_universe.definition: Overestimating the accuracy of one's predictive judgments, especially when information is coherent.

max_mode_universe.name: Illusion of transparency
max_mode_universe.definition: Overestimating the degree to which others know one's internal states.

max_mode_universe.name: Spotlight effect
max_mode_universe.definition: Overestimation of how much one is noticed by others.

max_mode_universe.name: Naive realism
max_mode_universe.definition: Belief that one perceives the world objectively, and that dissenters are biased, uninformed, or irrational.

max_mode_universe.name: Hostile attribution bias
max_mode_universe.definition: Tendency to interpret ambiguous behavior as hostile.

max_mode_universe.name: Confabulation (in decision records)
max_mode_universe.definition: Producing fabricated, distorted, or misinterpreted memories without intent to deceive.

max_mode_universe.name: Rosy retrospection
max_mode_universe.definition: Past events recalled more positively than they were judged at the time.

max_mode_universe.name: Telescoping effect
max_mode_universe.definition: Misremembering when events occurred.

max_mode_universe.name: Peak–end rule
max_mode_universe.definition: Judging experiences largely by their peak and their end.

max_mode_universe.name: Recency bias
max_mode_universe.definition: Over-weighting recent events relative to earlier ones.

max_mode_universe.name: Primacy effect
max_mode_universe.definition: First items in a sequence better remembered than middle items.

max_mode_universe.name: Gambler's fallacy
max_mode_universe.definition: Belief that independent events are affected by prior independent outcomes.

max_mode_universe.name: Hot-hand fallacy
max_mode_universe.definition: Belief that success breeds success in independent trials.

max_mode_universe.name: Regression-to-the-mean neglect
max_mode_universe.definition: Failure to anticipate that extreme observations will moderate.

max_mode_universe.name: Clustering illusion
max_mode_universe.definition: Seeing patterns in random data.

max_mode_universe.name: Conjunction fallacy
max_mode_universe.definition: Estimating a specific conjunction as more probable than one of its components.

max_mode_universe.name: Neglect of probability
max_mode_universe.definition: Disregarding probability information when under uncertainty.

max_mode_universe.name: Zero-risk bias
max_mode_universe.definition: Preferring to eliminate a small risk completely over reducing a larger risk substantially.

max_mode_universe.name: Denominator neglect
max_mode_universe.definition: Focusing on the numerator of a ratio and neglecting the denominator.

max_mode_universe.name: Ratio bias
max_mode_universe.definition: Larger-numerator ratios perceived as higher probability regardless of actual ratio.

max_mode_universe.name: Affect heuristic
max_mode_universe.definition: Using current emotion as a shortcut for risk/benefit judgment.

max_mode_universe.name: Negativity bias
max_mode_universe.definition: Negative information weighted more than equivalent positive information.

max_mode_universe.name: Positivity bias
max_mode_universe.definition: Favorable information weighted more than unfavorable.

max_mode_universe.name: Ostrich effect
max_mode_universe.definition: Avoidance of negative information.

max_mode_universe.name: Normalcy bias
max_mode_universe.definition: Underestimating the possibility or severity of a crisis because it has not yet occurred.

max_mode_universe.name: Dread risk bias
max_mode_universe.definition: Over-response to vivid low-probability risks relative to equivalently costly diffuse risks.

max_mode_universe.name: Risk compensation
max_mode_universe.definition: Behavior adjusts to perceived risk level, offsetting protective measures.

max_mode_universe.name: Observer-expectancy effect
max_mode_universe.definition: Researcher bias influences subjects or interpretation.

max_mode_universe.name: Experimenter's regress
max_mode_universe.definition: Difficulty separating what a result is from what it is taken to imply.

max_mode_universe.name: Belief bias
max_mode_universe.definition: Judging the strength of an argument by the believability of its conclusion.

max_mode_universe.name: Motivated reasoning
max_mode_universe.definition: Reasoning shaped by desired conclusions rather than by evidence.

max_mode_universe.name: Identity-protective cognition
max_mode_universe.definition: Processing information so as to protect one's social identity.

max_mode_universe.name: Belief perseverance
max_mode_universe.definition: Maintaining belief after the evidentiary basis has been discredited.

max_mode_universe.name: Continued influence effect
max_mode_universe.definition: Misinformation continues to influence reasoning after retraction.

max_mode_universe.name: Backfire effect (contested)
max_mode_universe.definition: Corrections sometimes strengthen the misperception they aim to correct. Effect is contested but documented in some conditions.

max_mode_universe.name: Escalation of commitment
max_mode_universe.definition: Increased investment in a course of action in response to its failure.

max_mode_universe.name: Narrative fallacy
max_mode_universe.definition: Imposing a coherent story on historical data where one is not warranted.

max_mode_universe.name: Texas sharpshooter fallacy
max_mode_universe.definition: Drawing the target around the clustered hits after the fact.

max_mode_universe.name: Goodhart's law as bias
max_mode_universe.definition: When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.

max_mode_universe.name: Streetlight effect
max_mode_universe.definition: Searching where it is easy, not where the answer is.

max_mode_universe.name: Parkinson's law of triviality
max_mode_universe.definition: Disproportionate deliberation on trivial items because they are understandable.

max_mode_universe.name: Zero-sum bias
max_mode_universe.definition: Tendency to view mixed-motive interactions as pure win/lose.

max_mode_universe.name: Reactive devaluation
max_mode_universe.definition: Proposals devalued because of who proposes them.

max_mode_universe.name: Not-invented-here syndrome
max_mode_universe.definition: Resistance to ideas originating outside the group.

max_mode_universe.name: Proportionality bias
max_mode_universe.definition: Big outcomes must have big causes.

max_mode_universe.name: Hyperbolic discounting
max_mode_universe.definition: Stronger preference for smaller-sooner over larger-later rewards.

max_mode_universe.name: Present bias
max_mode_universe.definition: Discounting future costs and benefits relative to present ones.

max_mode_universe.name: Projection bias
max_mode_universe.definition: Assuming future preferences will match current ones.

max_mode_universe.name: Focalism (focusing illusion)
max_mode_universe.definition: Overweighting a single salient factor.

max_mode_universe.name: Impact bias
max_mode_universe.definition: Overestimating the emotional impact of future events.

max_mode_universe.name: Empathy gap (hot/cold)
max_mode_universe.definition: Underestimating how future affective states will shift one's preferences.

max_mode_universe.name: Moral licensing
max_mode_universe.definition: Past good behavior licenses later problematic behavior.

max_mode_universe.name: Moral credentialing
max_mode_universe.definition: Claimed moral standing used to dismiss scrutiny.

max_mode_universe.name: System justification
max_mode_universe.definition: Defense of existing arrangements even when they disadvantage oneself or one's group.

max_mode_universe.name: Backfire through reactance

weak_multisource_signal_layer.name: Weak Multisource Signals Layer
weak_multisource_signal_layer.core_principle: Major government-management failures are often preceded by weak, distributed, heterogeneous signals. Each signal may be dismissible alone, but cross-source accumulation over time can indicate emerging CB/SF/MP/LCJ/LCC failure.

formalization.weak_signal: s_k = {source, environment, timestamp, strength, reliability, independence, mode_hypothesis}
formalization.multisource_signal_index: MSI(mode,t) = Σ reliability_k * strength_k * independence_k * environment_diversity_k * temporal_relevance_k
formalization.trigger_rule: if CEP(mode,t) exceeds threshold while individual signals remain below threshold -> early warning
formalization.cross_environment_diversity: number of distinct environments: operational, legal, audit, media, expert, social, procurement, citizen, sensor/data

anti_overclaim_rules: Weak signals are not proof of error.
Do not escalate a single low-quality weak signal without cross-source accumulation.
Always distinguish source reliability, signal strength and independence.
Treat social-media weak signals as hypothesis generators, not evidence by themselves.
Use weak signals to trigger investigation, not to declare guilt.

agent_contour_contribution_cluster_layer.name: Agent / Contour Contribution Clusters Layer
agent_contour_contribution_cluster_layer.core_principle: Government-management systems are heterogeneous. Errors often emerge not from a single actor, but from clusters formed by fragments of multiple governance contours: agencies, legal procedures, procurement channels, expert communities, political factions, media environments, social-media dynamics, and capacity mismatches. ACC identifies where the combined contribution to error activation is maximal.
agent_contour_contribution_cluster_layer.non_accusatory_disclaimer: ACC clusters are analytical contribution clusters. They do not establish legal guilt, criminal intent or moral blame. They identify where strategy, capacity, incentives, legal contour and weak signals jointly increase error probability.
agent_contour_contribution_cluster_layer.main_hypothesis: Across heterogeneous government-management contours, small contributions from different homo-agents and environments can accumulate into stable clusters. These clusters may become the true carriers of error, even when no single actor dominates alone.

formalization.cluster: C_k = {agents, groups, institutions, strategies, contours, weak_signals, modes}
formalization.cluster_error_mass: E(C_k) = Σ μ(mode_j) * contribution_weight_j over modes linked to cluster
formalization.cluster_shapley: φ(C_k) = average marginal contribution of cluster across coalition permutations
formalization.cluster_danger: Danger(C_k) = contribution * blocker_power * opacity * persistence * cross_environment_diversity
formalization.guilt_replacement: Use 'maximum contribution cluster' instead of 'guilty cluster'.

echo_room_group_dynamics_layer.name: Echo-room / Small-group Dynamics Layer
echo_room_group_dynamics_layer.core_principle: Inside government-management systems, important error-generating dynamics often happen in small groups, closed rooms, informal channels, inner circles and echo rooms. These settings can create hidden weak signals, suppress dissent, normalize anomalies and produce apparent consensus before formal procedure begins.
echo_room_group_dynamics_layer.central_assumption: For every high-stakes governance case, Errorlogy should assume the possible existence of hidden weak signals inside small-group dynamics and echo-room environments. This is an investigative prior, not proof. It triggers search for evidence of dissent, early warnings, anomalous reports, informal vetoes and briefing compression.
echo_room_group_dynamics_layer.public_language_rule: Do not say 'a hidden group definitely caused the error' without evidence. Say: 'small-group / echo-room dynamics are a plausible contribution channel; available evidence should be checked for hidden dissent, weak signals and informal consensus.'

formalization.hidden_signal_prior: P(hidden_WMS | closed_group, high_stakes, low_transparency, high_veto_power) > baseline
formalization.echo_room_pressure: ERP = closure * homogeneity * status_pressure * repetition * dissent_cost

fuzzy_predictive_dynamics_layer.name: Fuzzy Predictive Dynamics Layer
fuzzy_predictive_dynamics_layer.core_principle: Errorlogy forecasts are not claims of certain future events. They are fuzzy trajectories of error memberships, system regimes, weak-signal accumulation and contribution-cluster danger under stated assumptions.
fuzzy_predictive_dynamics_layer.central_question: How are errors, weak signals, contribution clusters and PNO regimes likely to evolve over time?
fuzzy_predictive_dynamics_layer.forecast_unit: trajectory of fuzzy membership μ_i(t), not binary true/false prediction
fuzzy_predictive_dynamics_layer.main_dynamic_equation: μ(t+1) = F(μ(t), α, WMS(t), ACC(t), EGD(t), LCC(t), LCJ(t), S_social(t), LBI_interventions(t))
fuzzy_predictive_dynamics_layer.continuous_time_equation: dμ_i/dt = activation_i + Σ_j α_{j→i} μ_j + WMS_i + ACC_i + EGD_i + LCC_i + LCJ_i - correction_i - decay_i + noise_i

Temporal compounding and legal/capacity lag can harden into persistent non-optimality.

Bad incentive equilibrium can defer externalities into long-term temporal failure.

anti_overclaim_rules: Forecasts are conditional trajectories, not deterministic predictions.
Always separate μ_forecast, scenario_probability, confidence and evidence_grade.
Do not present weak-signal warnings as proof of error.
Do not treat high cluster danger as legal guilt.
Always include assumptions and possible alternative explanations.
Backtest and recalibrate forecasts on retrospective cases before public deployment.
Use LBI counterfactuals to compare possible improvement paths, not to claim hindsight certainty.

integration.pipeline: data -> WMS -> μ modes -> α propagation -> ACC/EGD/LCC/LCJ state -> PNO scores -> FPD forecast -> LBI counterfactual -> LΩ residual analysis
